passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement, NutriBoost, on metabolic rate in adult mice. Twenty-four male C57BL/6 mice, aged 8 weeks, were randomly assigned to two groups: a control group receiving standard chow (n=12) and an experimental group receiving standard chow supplemented with 5% NutriBoost (n=12). Over a 6-week period, daily food intake and body weight were recorded. Metabolic rate was assessed weekly using indirect calorimetry, measuring oxygen consumption (VO2) and carbon dioxide production (VCO2). At the end of the study, mice were euthanized, and liver and adipose tissue samples were collected for histological analysis and gene expression profiling of key metabolic regulators (e.g., PPARα, UCP1). Preliminary data indicated that the experimental group exhibited an 11% increase in VO2 compared to controls, with no significant difference in food intake. Histology revealed increased brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity in the experimental group. Gene expression analysis showed upregulation of UCP1 and PPARα by 2.5-fold and 1.8-fold, respectively. These findings suggest that NutriBoost may enhance basal metabolic rate through activation of BAT and upregulation of thermogenic genes.

stem: Which parameter shows the greatest relative increase in the experimental group compared to the control group?
explanation: VO2 increased from 0.45 to 0.50 ml/min, a 11.1% rise, which is larger than the changes in VCO2 (10%), food intake (−3%), or body weight (−1.6%).
trap: A student might incorrectly choose VCO2 because it also increased, but the relative percent change is smaller.

stem: Which statement best describes the experimental design used in this study?
explanation: The investigators randomly assigned mice to a control or experimental group and manipulated the dietary supplement, fitting the definition of a randomized controlled trial.
trap: A student might choose an observational design because data were collected over time, but the key feature is random assignment and intervention.

stem: What is the percent increase in VO2 from the control to the experimental group?
explanation: Percent increase = (0.50 – 0.45) / 0.45 × 100 ≈ 11.1%. The closest answer is 11%.
trap: Students may round to 12% because the raw difference is 0.05, but the correct percent is 11.1%.

stem: Which of the following was held constant between the two groups in this study and therefore cannot explain the difference in VO2?

options.B: Presence of 5% NutriBoost in the diet

explanation: Correct: All 24 mice were male C57BL/6 aged 8 weeks, so sex is the same in both groups and cannot account for the VO2 difference. Why the others are wrong: B) The supplement is the one intended difference between the groups. C) BAT activity was reported to be higher in the experimental group. D) UCP1 was reported to be upregulated 2.5-fold in the experimental group.
trap: Treating any variable that could affect metabolism as a confounder even though it did not differ between groups.

stem: Which mechanism best explains how upregulation of UCP1 in brown adipose tissue can increase whole-animal oxygen consumption (VO₂)?

options.A: UCP1 dissipates the proton gradient, so electron transport and O₂ consumption rise while the energy is released as heat
options.B: UCP1 increases ATP synthase activity, so more ATP is made per O₂ consumed
options.C: UCP1 blocks the electron transport chain, which lowers O₂ use
options.D: UCP1 raises insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells

explanation: Correct: UCP1 uncouples respiration from ATP synthesis by letting protons re-enter the matrix, so the electron transport chain runs faster and consumes more O₂ while energy is released as heat. Why the others are wrong: B) UCP1 diverts protons away from ATP synthase, so it does not raise ATP made per O₂. C) UCP1 does not block electron transport; uncoupling speeds it. D) UCP1 is a mitochondrial protein in brown fat and has no role in insulin secretion.
trap: Confusing uncoupling with greater ATP production or with inhibition of the electron transport chain.
